items.extractedSnippet: What is hhw? Household hazardous waste can be any common household item Some of those half-used containers under your kitchen sink or tucked away in your garage could contain toxic chemicals that are harmful, or even deadly in certain circumstances. Some paints, cleaners, oils, batteries, and pesticides contain hazardous ingredients. Household hazardous waste, or HHW, is any chemical or product that can cause serious illness or pose an environmental or health threat if not properly stored, transported, or disposed of. Items can be purchased at home improvement stores, auto parts stores, supermarkets, yard and landscaping nurseries, and other similar places. This includes products that are corrosive or have the potential to react or combust. Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, mineral spirits, and furniture polish, are examples of substances that contain corrosive or potentially combustible ingredients. Household hazardous waste is dangerous because Items kept in the house can spill or leak, and children or pets could get into them. Containers thrown in the trash could end up in a landfill and get into the ground or ground water. Materials poured down the drain could damage public storm water drainage systems or make their way into wastewater treatment facilities. Some ingredients when not properly stored can turn corrosive or reactive. What we accept This is a sampling of some of the most common items customers bring to the center. The program requires leaves bagged in PAPER bags only (no plastic), with branches/other materials removed first — a specific, checkable logistical detail a homeowner would need to know before relying on it instead of a hauler.

(4) VISITOR BENEFIT — still only PLAUSIBLE, not proven: this does not establish how many real visitors are unaware of LeafDrop already or that adding it would measurably help anyone, since no analytics/Search Console data is available to this agent. Residents can download a coupon to receive a free five-pack of paper leaf bags at participating Ace Hardware stores . items.extractedSnippet: What is hhw? Household hazardous waste can be any common household item Some of those half-used containers under your kitchen sink or tucked away in your garage could contain toxic chemicals that are harmful, or even deadly in certain circumstances. Some paints, cleaners, oils, batteries, and pesticides contain hazardous ingredients. Household hazardous waste, or HHW, is any chemical or product that can cause serious illness or pose an environmental or health threat if not properly stored, transported, or disposed of. Items can be purchased at home improvement stores, auto parts stores, supermarkets, yard and landscaping nurseries, and other similar places. This includes products that are corrosive or have the potential to react or combust. Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, mineral spirits, and furniture polish, are examples of substances that contain corrosive or potentially combustible ingredients. Household hazardous waste is dangerous because Items kept in the house can spill or leak, and children or pets could get into them. Containers thrown in the trash could end up in a landfill and get into the ground or ground water. Materials poured down the drain could damage public storm water drainage systems or make their way into wastewater treatment facilities. Some ingredients when not properly stored can turn corrosive or reactive. What we accept This is a sampling of some of the most common items customers bring to the center. items.extractedSnippet: What is hhw? Household hazardous waste can be any common household item Some of those half-used containers under your kitchen sink or tucked away in your garage could contain toxic chemicals that are harmful, or even deadly in certain circumstances. Some paints, cleaners, oils, batteries, and pesticides contain hazardous ingredients. Household hazardous waste, or HHW, is any chemical or product that can cause serious illness or pose an environmental or health threat if not properly stored, transported, or disposed of. Items can be purchased at home improvement stores, auto parts stores, supermarkets, yard and landscaping nurseries, and other similar places. This includes products that are corrosive or have the potential to react or combust. Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, mineral spirits, and furniture polish, are examples of substances that contain corrosive or potentially combustible ingredients. Household hazardous waste is dangerous because Items kept in the house can spill or leak, and children or pets could get into them. Containers thrown in the trash could end up in a landfill and get into the ground or ground water. Materials poured down the drain could damage public storm water drainage systems or make their way into wastewater treatment facilities. Some ingredients when not properly stored can turn corrosive or reactive. What we accept This is a sampling of some of the most common items customers bring to the center. If you want to be sure that we can accept your items, search it on our Accepted Items page . Here are some of the main items that we do not accept . items.extractedSnippet: What is hhw? Household hazardous waste can be any common household item Some of those half-used containers under your kitchen sink or tucked away in your garage could contain toxic chemicals that are harmful, or even deadly in certain circumstances. Some paints, cleaners, oils, batteries, and pesticides contain hazardous ingredients. Household hazardous waste, or HHW, is any chemical or product that can cause serious illness or pose an environmental or health threat if not properly stored, transported, or disposed of. Items can be purchased at home improvement stores, auto parts stores, supermarkets, yard and landscaping nurseries, and other similar places. This includes products that are corrosive or have the potential to react or combust. Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, mineral spirits, and furniture polish, are examples of substances that contain corrosive or potentially combustible ingredients. Household hazardous waste is dangerous because Items kept in the house can spill or leak, and children or pets could get into them. Containers thrown in the trash could end up in a landfill and get into the ground or ground water. Materials poured down the drain could damage public storm water drainage systems or make their way into wastewater treatment facilities. Some ingredients when not properly stored can turn corrosive or reactive. What we accept This is a sampling of some of the most common items customers bring to the center. items.extractedSnippet: What is hhw? Household hazardous waste can be any common household item Some of those half-used containers under your kitchen sink or tucked away in your garage could contain toxic chemicals that are harmful, or even deadly in certain circumstances. Some paints, cleaners, oils, batteries, and pesticides contain hazardous ingredients. Household hazardous waste, or HHW, is any chemical or product that can cause serious illness or pose an environmental or health threat if not properly stored, transported, or disposed of. Items can be purchased at home improvement stores, auto parts stores, supermarkets, yard and landscaping nurseries, and other similar places. This includes products that are corrosive or have the potential to react or combust. Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, mineral spirits, and furniture polish, are examples of substances that contain corrosive or potentially combustible ingredients. Household hazardous waste is dangerous because Items kept in the house can spill or leak, and children or pets could get into them. Containers thrown in the trash could end up in a landfill and get into the ground or ground water. Materials poured down the drain could damage public storm water drainage systems or make their way into wastewater treatment facilities. Some ingredients when not properly stored can turn corrosive or reactive. What we accept This is a sampling of some of the most common items customers bring to the center. evidence: Denver runs an official free LeafDrop leaf/pumpkin composting drop-off program every fall (2026 run: October 5 - November 25), at three named city locations (Cherry Creek Transfer Station, Denver Parks and Recreation at 3685 Havana St, Central Platte Campus).

The program requires leaves bagged in PAPER bags only (no plastic), with branches/other materials removed first — a specific, checkable logistical detail a homeowner would need to know before relying on it instead of a hauler.

Mile High's existing seasonal-cleanout page mentions "Fall brings yard waste — branches, leaves, and general cleanup" but does not mention this municipal program at all, despite it being directly relevant to exactly the fall yard-waste scenario the page already discusses.

items.extractedSnippet: What is hhw? Household hazardous waste can be any common household item Some of those half-used containers under your kitchen sink or tucked away in your garage could contain toxic chemicals that are harmful, or even deadly in certain circumstances. Some paints, cleaners, oils, batteries, and pesticides contain hazardous ingredients. Household hazardous waste, or HHW, is any chemical or product that can cause serious illness or pose an environmental or health threat if not properly stored, transported, or disposed of. Items can be purchased at home improvement stores, auto parts stores, supermarkets, yard and landscaping nurseries, and other similar places. This includes products that are corrosive or have the potential to react or combust. Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, mineral spirits, and furniture polish, are examples of substances that contain corrosive or potentially combustible ingredients. Household hazardous waste is dangerous because Items kept in the house can spill or leak, and children or pets could get into them. Containers thrown in the trash could end up in a landfill and get into the ground or ground water. Materials poured down the drain could damage public storm water drainage systems or make their way into wastewater treatment facilities. Some ingredients when not properly stored can turn corrosive or reactive. What we accept This is a sampling of some of the most common items customers bring to the center. items.extractedSnippet: What is hhw? Household hazardous waste can be any common household item Some of those half-used containers under your kitchen sink or tucked away in your garage could contain toxic chemicals that are harmful, or even deadly in certain circumstances. Some paints, cleaners, oils, batteries, and pesticides contain hazardous ingredients. Household hazardous waste, or HHW, is any chemical or product that can cause serious illness or pose an environmental or health threat if not properly stored, transported, or disposed of. Items can be purchased at home improvement stores, auto parts stores, supermarkets, yard and landscaping nurseries, and other similar places. This includes products that are corrosive or have the potential to react or combust. Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, mineral spirits, and furniture polish, are examples of substances that contain corrosive or potentially combustible ingredients. Household hazardous waste is dangerous because Items kept in the house can spill or leak, and children or pets could get into them. Containers thrown in the trash could end up in a landfill and get into the ground or ground water. Materials poured down the drain could damage public storm water drainage systems or make their way into wastewater treatment facilities. Some ingredients when not properly stored can turn corrosive or reactive. What we accept This is a sampling of some of the most common items customers bring to the center. Household hazardous waste can be any common household item Some of those half-used containers under your kitchen sink or tucked away in your garage could contain toxic chemicals that are harmful, or even deadly in certain circumstances. Some paints, cleaners, oils, batteries, and pesticides contain hazardous ingredients. Household hazardous waste, or HHW, is any chemical or product that can cause serious illness or pose an environmental or health threat if not properly stored, transported, or disposed of. Items can be purchased at home improvement stores, auto parts stores, supermarkets, yard and landscaping nurseries, and other similar places. This includes products that are corrosive or have the potential to react or combust. Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, mineral spirits, and furniture polish, are examples of substances that contain corrosive or potentially combustible ingredients. Household hazardous waste is dangerous because Items kept in the house can spill or leak, and children or pets could get into them. Containers thrown in the trash could end up in a landfill and get into the ground or ground water. Materials poured down the drain could damage public storm water drainage systems or make their way into wastewater treatment facilities. Some ingredients when not properly stored can turn corrosive or reactive. What we accept This is a sampling of some of the most common items customers bring to the center. evidence: Denver runs an official free LeafDrop leaf/pumpkin composting drop-off program every fall (2026 run: October 5 - November 25), at three named city locations (Cherry Creek Transfer Station, Denver Parks and Recreation at 3685 Havana St, Central Platte Campus).

The program requires leaves bagged in PAPER bags only (no plastic), with branches/other materials removed first — a specific, checkable logistical detail a homeowner would need to know before relying on it instead of a hauler.

Mile High's existing seasonal-cleanout page mentions "Fall brings yard waste — branches, leaves, and general cleanup" but does not mention this municipal program at all, despite it being directly relevant to exactly the fall yard-waste scenario the page already discusses.

(3) EVERGREEN-CONTENT RISK — LeafDrop's dates/locations are set annually by the city and are NOT safe to hardcode as static page copy with no maintenance plan; if this is acted on, the published wording should describe the PROGRAM generically ("the city runs a seasonal free leaf drop-off program each fall") and link to Denver's own LeafDrop page for the current year's specific dates/locations, rather than embedding "October 5 - November 25" as evergreen text that will be wrong next year. Also, as before: does NOT establish search volume or ranking impact — SERP/news presence is not the same as demonstrated visitor demand.

The program requires leaves bagged in PAPER bags only (no plastic), with branches/other materials removed first — a specific, checkable logistical detail a homeowner would need to know before relying on it instead of a hauler.

items.extractedSnippet: What is hhw? Household hazardous waste can be any common household item Some of those half-used containers under your kitchen sink or tucked away in your garage could contain toxic chemicals that are harmful, or even deadly in certain circumstances. Some paints, cleaners, oils, batteries, and pesticides contain hazardous ingredients. Household hazardous waste, or HHW, is any chemical or product that can cause serious illness or pose an environmental or health threat if not properly stored, transported, or disposed of. Items can be purchased at home improvement stores, auto parts stores, supermarkets, yard and landscaping nurseries, and other similar places. This includes products that are corrosive or have the potential to react or combust. Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, mineral spirits, and furniture polish, are examples of substances that contain corrosive or potentially combustible ingredients. Household hazardous waste is dangerous because Items kept in the house can spill or leak, and children or pets could get into them. Containers thrown in the trash could end up in a landfill and get into the ground or ground water. Materials poured down the drain could damage public storm water drainage systems or make their way into wastewater treatment facilities. Some ingredients when not properly stored can turn corrosive or reactive. What we accept This is a sampling of some of the most common items customers bring to the center. items.extractedSnippet: What is hhw? Household hazardous waste can be any common household item Some of those half-used containers under your kitchen sink or tucked away in your garage could contain toxic chemicals that are harmful, or even deadly in certain circumstances. Some paints, cleaners, oils, batteries, and pesticides contain hazardous ingredients. Household hazardous waste, or HHW, is any chemical or product that can cause serious illness or pose an environmental or health threat if not properly stored, transported, or disposed of. Items can be purchased at home improvement stores, auto parts stores, supermarkets, yard and landscaping nurseries, and other similar places. This includes products that are corrosive or have the potential to react or combust. Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, mineral spirits, and furniture polish, are examples of substances that contain corrosive or potentially combustible ingredients. Household hazardous waste is dangerous because Items kept in the house can spill or leak, and children or pets could get into them. Containers thrown in the trash could end up in a landfill and get into the ground or ground water. Materials poured down the drain could damage public storm water drainage systems or make their way into wastewater treatment facilities. Some ingredients when not properly stored can turn corrosive or reactive. What we accept This is a sampling of some of the most common items customers bring to the center. items.extractedSnippet: LeafDrop and Pumpkin Recycling LeafDrop and Pumpkin Recycling Denver's LeafDrop program allows residents to dispose of their fall leaves in an environmentally friendly way. Each fall, Denver's Office of the City Forester partners with Denver's Department of Transportation & Infrastructure (DOTI), Denver's Office of Climate Action, Sustainability and Resiliency (CASR) and Ace Hardware to provide paper leaf bags and designated drop-off sites for Denver residents. Loose leaves and compostable leaf bags are also accepted in Denver's green compost carts. Residents can download a coupon to receive a free five-pack of paper leaf bags at participating Ace Hardware stores . Leaves dropped off in plastic bags must be emptied on site. 2026 Drop Sites WEEKDAY DROP SITES: Oct. 5 - Nov. 25 The following LeafDrop locations will be open on weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m.: Cherry Creek Transfer Station* - 7301 E. items.extractedSnippet: What is hhw? Household hazardous waste can be any common household item Some of those half-used containers under your kitchen sink or tucked away in your garage could contain toxic chemicals that are harmful, or even deadly in certain circumstances. Some paints, cleaners, oils, batteries, and pesticides contain hazardous ingredients. Household hazardous waste, or HHW, is any chemical or product that can cause serious illness or pose an environmental or health threat if not properly stored, transported, or disposed of. Items can be purchased at home improvement stores, auto parts stores, supermarkets, yard and landscaping nurseries, and other similar places. This includes products that are corrosive or have the potential to react or combust. Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, mineral spirits, and furniture polish, are examples of substances that contain corrosive or potentially combustible ingredients. Household hazardous waste is dangerous because Items kept in the house can spill or leak, and children or pets could get into them. Containers thrown in the trash could end up in a landfill and get into the ground or ground water. Materials poured down the drain could damage public storm water drainage systems or make their way into wastewater treatment facilities. Some ingredients when not properly stored can turn corrosive or reactive. What we accept This is a sampling of some of the most common items customers bring to the center. If you want to be sure that we can accept your items, search it on our Accepted Items page . Here are some of the main items that we do not accept . research.source: City and County of Denver — Department of Transportation and Infrastructure, LeafDrop program (denvergov.org); corroborated by Denver Gazette (2026-10-11) and Denverite coverage of the same program
evidence: Denver runs an official free LeafDrop leaf/pumpkin composting drop-off program every fall (2026 run: October 5 - November 25), at three named city locations (Cherry Creek Transfer Station, Denver Parks and Recreation at 3685 Havana St, Central Platte Campus).

The program requires leaves bagged in PAPER bags only (no plastic), with branches/other materials removed first — a specific, checkable logistical detail a homeowner would need to know before relying on it instead of a hauler.

items.extractedSnippet: LeafDrop and Pumpkin Recycling LeafDrop and Pumpkin Recycling Denver's LeafDrop program allows residents to dispose of their fall leaves in an environmentally friendly way. Each fall, Denver's Office of the City Forester partners with Denver's Department of Transportation & Infrastructure (DOTI), Denver's Office of Climate Action, Sustainability and Resiliency (CASR) and Ace Hardware to provide paper leaf bags and designated drop-off sites for Denver residents. Loose leaves and compostable leaf bags are also accepted in Denver's green compost carts. Residents can download a coupon to receive a free five-pack of paper leaf bags at participating Ace Hardware stores . items.extractedSnippet: What is hhw? Household hazardous waste can be any common household item Some of those half-used containers under your kitchen sink or tucked away in your garage could contain toxic chemicals that are harmful, or even deadly in certain circumstances. Some paints, cleaners, oils, batteries, and pesticides contain hazardous ingredients. Household hazardous waste, or HHW, is any chemical or product that can cause serious illness or pose an environmental or health threat if not properly stored, transported, or disposed of. Items can be purchased at home improvement stores, auto parts stores, supermarkets, yard and landscaping nurseries, and other similar places. This includes products that are corrosive or have the potential to react or combust. Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, mineral spirits, and furniture polish, are examples of substances that contain corrosive or potentially combustible ingredients. Household hazardous waste is dangerous because Items kept in the house can spill or leak, and children or pets could get into them. Containers thrown in the trash could end up in a landfill and get into the ground or ground water. Materials poured down the drain could damage public storm water drainage systems or make their way into wastewater treatment facilities. Some ingredients when not properly stored can turn corrosive or reactive. What we accept This is a sampling of some of the most common items customers bring to the center. If you want to be sure that we can accept your items, search it on our Accepted Items page . Here are some of the main items that we do not accept .
